https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text: ‘The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them.’ Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters View image in fullscreen ‘The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them.’ Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters AI (artificial intelligence) OpenAI to pause some work on AI model Astra due to security concerns Agent found to be able to find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, and to carry out cyber-attacks Eric Berger Sat 8 Aug 2026 13.00 EDT First published on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google OpenAI will pause some work on an artificial intelligence model because of security concerns, the company stated Friday, following a series of incidents in which AI agents have escaped containment. The company had evaluated the agent, Astra, and found “significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity”, which had moved to a “critical” threshold where it can find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, or devise and execute cyber-attacks when given only a “high level desired goal”. OpenAI stated that the model was not involved in an incident in which one of its AI agents went rogue during a test, accessed the open web and hacked a startup, Hugging Face. The company discovered other instances in which autonomous agents had escaped containment, Reuters reported in July. The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them. Still, critics of the AI industry have warned that such disclosures from OpenAI and its competitors Anthropic and Meta could be designed to generate hype about the technology’s power and thus spur additional interest from investors. To prevent potential rogue behavior from AI agents, OpenAI is “implementing stricter security controls for higher-capability models and associated activities, including isolated testing environments, restricted network and tool access”, the company’s blog post stated. It will also install “enhanced model weight protections and encryption, additional monitoring and detection capabilities”. The company will pause internal activities involving Astra that do not meet these new requirements. “We’re committed to working alongside governments, safety institutes, and civil society to ensure that the frontier capabilities of models like Astra, and those that follow, are deployed responsibly and broadly for the benefit of all humanity,” the company stated. Meta also disclosed this week that one of its models hacked another company during cybersecurity testing. And the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) announced on 4 August that agents powered by OpenAI and Anthropic had sent targeted emails to software developers in an attempt to pass a cyber challenge. “These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world,” the institute stated in a blog post. The organisation cautioned that the models’ sending of harmful software was not a case of a “model escaping its secure test environment” but rather that the group had intentionally permitted internet access to “best assess the maximum capability of models”. Still, the “behaviour was possible, sustained, and new; that alone warrants attention”, AISI said. The reports emerged while the Trump administration was finalizing a framework on how to test AI models for safety and cybersecurity risks. OpenAI and Anthropic, which have increased competition from China and other tech firms, have argued that open-source models, meaning those that allow anyone to see and modify the underlying program code, pose a security risk and pushed for additional federal regulations on them. https://www.politico.eu/article/volodymy.text: PRISTINA — Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s weekend trip to Serbia triggered reverberations in the Balkans long after the Ukrainian president jetted back to Kyiv. Zelenskyy visited Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić — who has refused to join the EU’s sanctions regime against Russia and maintains a cozy relationship with the Kremlin — for the first time on Saturday. He then waded into the thorniest regional dispute by declaring Ukraine would continue not to recognize the independence of Kosovo, a former province of Serbia. Kosovo’s response was swift. A building-sized blue-and-yellow “Free Ukraine” banner that has been up on Pristina’s main thoroughfare since 2022 came down immediately, with Mayor Përparim Rama declaring that while his sympathies remain with “peoples facing war, violence and persecution … respect must be mutual.” Advertisement Advertisement Since Zelenskyy’s visit, Vučić threatened to physically redirect the Iber River that runs from Serbia to Kosovo in retaliation for Kosovo demolishing Serb-owned houses along the reservoir’s shore. Such a move would drain the reservoir supplying much of Kosovo’s water and crucial cooling capacity to its largest power plant. In addition, Serbian Foreign Minister Marko Djurić and Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama exchanged barbs on X, with the latter accusing Serbia of being in “a political bubble” and being in denial over the fact that “Serbia lost Kosova” long ago. Kosovo was an Albanian-majority southern province of Serbia for most of the 20th century. Its people held broad political rights under socialist Yugoslavia until a decade-long Serb crackdown on dissent led to the armed conflict of 1998-99. A three-month NATO bombing campaign drove Serbian forces out and made the province a U.N. protectorate. Kosovo declared independence in 2008 and, to date, it is recognized by over 100 nations, including the U.S., U.K. and 22 of the 27 EU member countries. It is also a potential EU candidate country, submitting its application in December 2022. The country’s status has long been a favorite talking point for Russian President Vladimir Putin, who has used it to justify invading Georgia in 2008 and annexing Crimea in 2014. Kosovo’s Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca said he took note of Zelenskyy’s views “with regret” and that such rhetoric echoes “Russia’s attempts to invoke Kosova as a precedent.” As for why Ukraine’s leader would wade into the intractable Balkan issue at all, it likely comes down to weaponry. Advertisement Advertisement Serbia still produces considerable quantities of ammunition in the Soviet-standard calibers which would be impossible to acquire from Kyiv’s Western allies, who use the NATO standard instead. Ukraine retains Soviet-era heavy howitzers and tanks that remain key to the fight in the Donbas and beyond. And despite his pro-Russian stance, Vučić is happy to provide them to Kyiv quietly. “Ukraine is in a position where it cannot care about things beyond the more immediate needs for Ukraine, and Vučić matters to him more,” explained Florian Bieber, who directs the Centre for Southeast European Studies at the University of Graz. Vučić’s overtures towards Zelenskyy could be in part an effort to placate criticism from Brussels . EU leaders have condemned the “explosion of violence” during the ongoing anti-government protest movement and the “collapse in democratic standards” in Serbia. “He’s hoping that he will get less critical remarks in the coming months because of his close, at least symbolically closer, ties with Zelenskyy. Vučić is doing this for leverage with the EU ahead of possible elections in the country,” Bieber continued. Kosovo’s supporters have long cast its independence as a one-off, not a template. But the circumstances of its journey away from Serbia remains divisive, particularly for EU members like Spain and Cyprus, who have their own separatist headaches and still refuse to recognize Kosovo’s independence. “Depending on which side of this argument you’re coming down on, you will have a different view over what Kosovo’s independence means for other conflicts and other territorial disputes around the world,” said Bieber. http://www.parisguardian.com/news/279216.text: Warsaw blames Moscow after a missile crashes in Poland France24 30 Jul 2026, 19:33 GMT+10 Polandsaid Thursday that a missile that blasted a 10-metre (33 feet) crater inside its territory was likely fired byRussiain its latest mass attack onUkraine. Read moreRussian strikes across Ukraine kill at least 8, wound more than a dozen NATOand European leaders openly blamed Russia for the 4am (0200 GMT) explosion in a field that shook residents of the village of Tarnawa Kolonia, 80 kilometres (50 miles) from the border, and the windows of their homes. The massive hole and debris were found in a field two kilometres away, police said. "From the analysis of most of the traces, the recovered fragments point to a Russian Kh-101 missile," Prime Minister Donald Tusk told a news conference near the crater. "There is no reason to think that Poland was the target," he said, but added that two "objects" had violated Polands airspace. "One of them definitely did, because we have its traces here, and the other was near the Polish border, but it was a very brief signal, so there were no consequences associated with it." Poland a member of NATO and theEuropean Unionhas experienced repeat incursions by missiles and drones during Russia's war on Ukraine since 2022. NATO activation The latest missile fell as Russia staged a massive deadly attack on the Lviv region in western Ukraine, near the border with Poland. Tusk chaired a crisis unit meeting with Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz and Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski in Lublin, the nearest city to the village. A military prosecutor's investigation has been opened to determine the origin and nature of the explosion. NATO, Ukraine and European leaders strongly condemned Russia for breaching Poland's airspace. A NATO spokesman, Martin O'Donnell, said: "In response to a Russian missile of currently unknown type that entered Polish airspace and later crashed into Polish territory one of many missiles fired by Russia at Ukraine overnight NATO and Poland activated their air and ground defences." He added that alliance commanders were "in close contact with the Polish authorities about the violation of Poland's airspace. This intrusion "reminds us that there is nothing more urgent for our two countries than to counter our common, age-old enemy, which represents a direct threat to both our nations", Ukrainian foreign minister Andriy Sybiga wrote on X, referring to Russia's attacks. A Polish F-16 fighter jet took off after the missile was detected but lost track of it, authorities initially indicated. Tusk said Polish air defence would have shot down the missile if it had deviated from its trajectory and headed toward populated areas. In a message on X addressed to Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyand Tusk, French PresidentEmmanuel Macroncondemned "in the strongest possible terms the Russian strikes that killed civilians in Ukraine, as well as the violation of Polish airspace". "Our support for Ukraine and our allies will not weaken," he wrote. "The Polish people are famously unafraid ... and our thoughts are with them," EU Commission presidentUrsula von der Leyenwrote on X as she condemned the Russian attack. "To put an end to this, we are helping Ukraine win this war in every way we can," she added. During the night, Russia launched 74 missiles and 284 drones at Ukraine, killing at least eight people. In November 2022, a Ukrainian air-defence missile fell on the Polish village of Przewodow, killing two people. And in September 2025, around 20 Russian drones that entered Polish airspace were shot down or crashed. Other European states have also been hit by Russian drones and missiles since 2022, particularlyRomaniaandMoldova. The pair worked together for three decades, with Griffiths saying Denton was a ‘true clown and much beloved’. Photograph: James Penlidis Photography Australian books Terry Denton, beloved Australian illustrator best known for Treehouse series, dies aged 76 The illustrator and author ‘gave joy to millions of children around the world’, his family says Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Guardian staff Tue 22 Sep 2026 04.16 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 04.43 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The beloved Australian illustrator and author Terry Denton, most famous for his work on the Treehouse series, has died aged 76. His publisher, Curtis Brown, released a statement on social media saying Denton died surrounded by his family on Monday. Denton was the author and illustrator of more than 30 of his own books, including the Gasp! series, which was adapted for screen. He also collaborated with authors including Mem Fox, Paul Jennings and Gillian Rubinstein. This ‘bum-poo-fart author’ is Australia’s biggest writer: Andy Griffiths on ending the Treehouse books Read more Denton’s children paid tribute to the illustrator whose work they said “gave joy to millions of children around the world”. “And after all those stories and all those lives he touched, he always came home to us. “We are so grateful that his stories will continue to live on, bringing wonder, laughter and comfort to generations yet to come and most especially to his beloved grandchildren, whoever will grow up knowing him through the magic he left behind.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Andy Griffiths, the author of the Treehouse series and a longtime friend and collaborator with Denton, said: “Working – and playing – with Terry over three decades has been an incredible honour and a pure delight. “I’ve never laughed so hard as I did when working with him, whether in the writing room or on stage. He was a true clown and much beloved – both in real life and as a character in the Treehouse series. Jill and I will miss him greatly.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Griffiths told the Guardian in 2023 that he owed much of his success to the talented illustrator. When he first searched for a publisher, he had little luck but one took a punt on a textbook that was published in 1993 and was illustrated by Denton. Griffiths said that when they met for the first time, they recognised a streak of madness in each other that would fuel the next 30 years of work together. Denton is survived by his wife, Kristen, his children Max, Imogen and Eve, and his grandchildren Georgia, Lucy, Charlie, Alfie and Felix.
